title: Adjectives and agreement

objectives.can: Match an adjective to its noun in case, number and gender, whatever their declensions.

explanation.summary: A Latin adjective agrees with the noun it describes in case, number and gender. It does not copy the noun's ending: it has its own set of endings, and the two words often end differently. Agreement is what lets Latin put an adjective far from its noun and still be understood.

sections.heading: Agreement is of case, number and gender
body: In *vitam æternam* both words are accusative singular feminine. In *Pater meus* both are nominative singular masculine. The adjective takes whatever case, number and gender its noun has, and chooses from its own endings to show it.

That is why an adjective can end differently from its noun. The adjective in *dies Domini magnus* ends in -us like a second-declension masculine, although *dies* belongs to the fifth declension. The adjective in *semini tuo* has the second-declension ending -o, although *semen* is third declension and neuter. Agreement means the same case, number and gender, not the same ending.

sections.heading: Adjectives of the first and second declensions
body: The largest group of adjectives has three sets of endings: masculine like *dominus*, feminine like *terra*, neuter like *verbum*. The dictionary lists them as three forms: *magnus, magna, magnum* (great); *novus, nova, novum* (new). The masculine and neuter use the second-declension endings you know, the feminine the first. A few have the masculine in -er, but the endings are the same.

The possessives *meus* (my), *tuus* (your, singular) work in the same way. They are adjectives, so they agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner: *Pater meus*, 'my Father', is masculine because *pater* is masculine, not because the speaker is.

sections.heading: Adjectives of the third declension
body: Other adjectives use the third-declension endings. In the commonest kind the masculine and feminine are alike, and only the neuter differs: *fortis* (strong), *fidelis* (faithful). Dictionaries give *fortis, forte*. A few have one form for all three genders in the nominative singular: *omnipotens*, genitive *omnipotentis*. These are looked up by the genitive, as third-declension nouns are.

A third-declension adjective can describe a noun of any declension, and the noun's declension can differ from the adjective's. Only case, number and gender must match. The ablative singular of such adjectives is -i or -e; you will meet both. When the form alone is ambiguous, look at the noun beside it.

sections.heading: Adjectives standing as nouns
body: A Latin adjective can stand alone and act as a noun, with its gender and number telling what it stands for. A masculine plural means 'people who are such': *fideles*, 'the faithful'. A neuter plural means 'things which are such'. A masculine singular can mean 'the one who is such': in Isaiah, *Sanctus Israël* is 'the Holy One of Israel'.

Where an adjective stands alone, ask what it must agree with, and what the gender and number suggest: masculine for persons, neuter for things. Often the verse has a noun elsewhere to which it belongs, and sometimes it has none.

sections.heading: Position and the predicate
body: An adjective may stand before or after its noun; neither order is a rule. Emphasis and style decide. It may also be the predicate: *Ego sum vitis vera* has the adjective with the verb *sum*, and *quoniam bonus* is a whole clause. In that case it still agrees with the subject, which may be left out.

misunderstandings: Agreement does not mean the endings match. An -a on an adjective is not a sign that the noun ends in -a. Find the noun's case, number and gender first, then check that the adjective shows the same ones.
A third-declension noun can have a first/second-declension adjective, and the other way round. *homo bonus* is normal.
The gender of an adjective is the gender of its noun, not a fixed property of the adjective. The same adjective appears as *magnus*, *magna* or *magnum* according to the noun it describes.
The possessive follows the thing possessed, not the owner. *Pater meus* is masculine because *pater* is masculine, not because the speaker is male.

deeper.heading: Undecided forms in an adjective
body: Adjective endings overlap even more than noun endings, as the table shows: -o is dative and ablative, -a is nominative singular feminine and nominative or accusative neuter plural, and -is is dative and ablative in all genders. The library's analysis often leaves the gender of an adjective undecided for that reason. The questions below therefore ask mainly about case and number, and ask for the gender only where the form leaves no doubt.
